reading.body:
CyrusOne's Sterling campus holds 44 MW of IT capacity across 420,000 square feet, ranking 12th among the 25 Virginia data centers that publish power figures.

Virginia has 330 mapped data center facilities, but only 25 publish a power specification. Those 25 account for the state's announced 1,603 MW of IT load, and Sterling alone is 2.7% of it. The published picture of Virginia capacity is therefore a small, self-selected sample, and a campus this size still lands mid-tier within it.

For AI specifically, the useful number is density. At 40 kW per rack, a typical AI training figure, 44 MW implies roughly 1,100 racks of compute. That is a real but not decisive quantity of accelerators, and it is an inference from an assumed density rather than a published rack count. The campus carries certifications for financial, healthcare, and federal workloads, which says it can host regulated tenants, not that it hosts AI ones.

What the data does not cover is the part that decides the question. Tenant mix, actual power draw, and whether any capacity is allocated to training or inference are all unpublished. The suitability score of 70 is built from published IT capacity and operator type, and it flags announced expansion as missing. Sterling's relevance to AI scaling cannot be settled from what is disclosed here.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
